The green field was simply a flood of maroon jerseys flooding forward engulfing Blue traffic-cones. Veteran fullback James Tedesco scores the match-winner for NSW on Wednesday night. Getty Images And what did Laurie Daley see? He saw a team whose defence was round-heeled, whose attack was close to non-existent who were so bad they appeared to be either boozed or bamboozled. Seriously, were they drunk, or just confused? And has there ever been a more disastrous opening stanza from a team in State of Origin?



I repeat: 20 minutes in, the Blues were down 20-0 and the game was over – it was just a question of how bad the pantsing would be from there. Emblematic of their dominance was the opening try, just a few minutes in. Sam Walker had the ball on a string, and dribbled the ball through the Sydney drizzle with superbly judged weight. The ball skidded loose, every Blue jersey frozen in uncertainty. Into that back-field of Blues statues flew Robert Toia, the debutant Blues centre arriving exactly where history says its heroes must arrive - first. The next try was even better. Queensland maestro Harry Grant hit the line just five metres from the Blues posts and did something so rare it doesn’t even have a name, so we’ll have to call it a “no-look reverse-flick off-load.” The ball went to Walker and then a rampaging Thomas Flegler, who seemed uncertain how the ball got into his hands but put it down anyway. Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow celebrates his try before things turned sour for Queensland. NRL Photo



The Blues had barely finished arguing with themselves when Queensland decided it was time to put the Hammer down. The Maroons swept left, the ball was kicked through and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow found himself in enough space to make Neil Armstrong feel at home. He accelerated on to it, gathered the ball in, and put it down for a beauty! Twenty-nil! Related Article Analysis

State of Origin Origin I looked over after 20 minutes. The Ponga send-off changed everything The Queenslanders were not merely winning; they were conducting a masterclass in how it’s done. Beyond the tries, it was clear that the north-of-the-Tweed-ers were bigger, faster, harder, and more committed. In every set of six, they were making nigh on 50 per cent more metres than their opponents! Great Blues players had shockingly ordinary games. Brian To’o could barely take a pass. Stephen Crichton could barely take a trick. Mercifully, one bit of Nathan Cleary magic saw Hudson Young score to make it 20-6 just before half-time, but it really was clear the game was over. And then halfway through the second half, Maroons fullback Kalyn Ponga was sensationally sent off for a high shot. The game changed in an instant!



Related Article State of Origin How Sam Walker silenced his critics in controversial Origin debut Six minutes later, Crichton came alive to put Ethan Strange over in the corner, and it was back to 20-10, with the conversion missed. The Blues couldn’t, could they? It seemed not, as they butchered no fewer than three – count ’em, THREE - tries. But now Cleary takes the matter in hand, with the ball in the same, straightening, accelerating, and attacking the line. For an instant, there was hesitation among the Maroons, the smallest pause, the briefest uncertainty, and Cleary goes through! 20-16.



And you know the rest. For if you haven’t already seen it 10 times, not to worry – you’ll see it 50 times in the next few days. After superb lead-up work by the entire team, James Tedesco miraculously gathers in a Cleary bomb to go over just to the left of the posts. Cleary converts his successful bomb with aplomb, to pull off the great escape in style 22-20. I am not sure the best team won on the night. But it was certainly the best escape in modern memory.

World.title: Origin I looked over after 20 minutes. The Ponga send-off changed everything
World.content:
Analysis SportNRLState of Origin Origin I looked over after 20 minutes. The Ponga send-off changed everything Tom Decent May 27, 2026 — 11:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

The sight of Jai Arrow walking off the Queensland team bus in a Maroons blazer on Wednesday night was enough to send shivers down the spine of Blues fans. It was a powerful moment, akin to last year when Cameron Munster declared he would play in the Origin decider in Sydney just three days after the death of his father, Steven. We all know how that movie ended: a stunning 24-12 Queensland victory fuelled by a playmaker with the ball on a string and a greater purpose driving him. Loading Arrow’s battle with motor neurone disease has rocked the rugby league world, and the Maroons were able to draw on a hefty dose of old-fashioned Queensland spirit in a match that looked over after 20 minutes. Queensland displayed all the traits Arrow will need in his battle – courage, determination and resilience – as they carved open a shaky Blues outfit whose ball handling was diabolical.



That was until Kalyn Ponga was sent off and all hell broke loose, as James Tedesco leapt high in the air in the penultimate minute for one of the greatest Origin tries in the greatest comeback in Origin history. Somehow, the Blues found themselves in front by full-time, in one of the most incredible games of rugby league imaginable. James Tedesco gives NSW a stunning victory in the Origin series opener. Getty Images Nathan Cleary answered his critics in the most emphatic fashion with a clutch 40-20 and outstanding leadership as the Blues ran over the top of a wounded 12-man Maroons outfit to win 22-20 with a conversion in the final five seconds. For all the debate about whether Billy Slater made the wrong call by picking Ponga over Reece Walsh, the decision seemed to be vindicated in a breathtaking first half as the Newcastle star threw audacious passes deep inside Queensland territory and flew to take high balls with little regard for his own safety.



That was until Ponga’s second-half send-off changed the complexion of the match as the Blues saw an opening and broke the visitors’ hearts. The Maroons have won countless Origin matches with an inferior team on paper, continually finding a way to squeeze more juice out of the lemon through internal and external motivations. Their spine of Munster, Ponga, Sam Walker and Harry Grant looked to make a mockery of the bookmakers before the Blues rebounded in magnificent style to take a 1-0 series lead against all the odds. Ashley Klein’s decision to send off Kalyn Ponga changed the game. Getty Images The best players can flick a switch on the biggest occasions, and Ponga and Munster did exactly that, particularly the latter given his patchy club form with Melbourne to the point he had even apparently contemplated retirement a few weeks ago. The taunt that Queensland “get” Origin didn’t come to fruition when it mattered most as the Blues’ spine of Cleary, Tedesco, Ethan Strange and Reece Robson found cohesion, creativity and control right at the death.



It was fitting Cleary and his new halves partner Strange stood arm in arm during the national anthem, as it proved a symbol of the partnership that followed over the next 80 minutes, with flashes of individual brilliance from both. What a refreshing sight it was to see some flow return to rugby league as referee Ashley Klein largely put away his whistle. League great Andrew Johns had foreshadowed all week that Walker’s short kicking game loomed as a major threat, and his pinpoint grubber to set up Roosters teammate Robert Toia was an ominous sign of what was to come. Cleary orchestrated one of the great grand final first halves at the same venue against Parramatta in 2022, but on Wednesday night he found himself on the receiving end of one of Queensland’s best opening salvos. Or perhaps it was simply one of NSW’s worst, as evidenced by a completion rate of just 44 per cent after 25 minutes.



Cleary’s final quarter had shades of his masterclass in the 2023 grand final against Brisbane, while Tedesco’s outstanding late try was better than his effort for NSW to steal victory in 2019. Related Article NSW 22 Queensland 20

NRL 2026 Tedesco stunner hands NSW the biggest comeback win in Origin history As the carnage unfolded and the Blues trailed 20-0, Victor Radley stood near the bench with hands on hips waiting for his opportunity, like a caged lion watching every chance at a kill slip by. NSW scored in the first set after he entered the field, but their ill-discipline for the remainder of the night repeatedly left coach Laurie Daley rocking his head back and burying his face in his hands. By the end of the night, Daley was all smiles, as stunned as anyone that the Blues had clawed their way back against all the odds. “I don’t know how coaches do that week in, week out,” a drained Daley said.

World.title: Coached by Canberra’s greatest five-eighth, Strange makes a dream Origin debut
World.content:
SportNRLState of Origin Coached by Canberra’s greatest five-eighth, Strange makes a dream Origin debut Chris Barrett May 27, 2026 — 10:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Compared to the most famous of Canberra five-eighths, Ethan Strange entered his first State of Origin match with high hopes of living up to the exploits of Laurie Daley. He has a long way to match Daley’s achievements as a player, but his debut was fair start. Loading The 21-year-old Raider was a revelation in the Blues’ astounding come-from-behind victory at Accor Stadium on Wednesday night. Not bad for someone who was only called into the starting side on the eve of the game.



Strange scored a try himself and was denied a second by an obstruction as NSW steamed back into the game in the last 20 minutes against a 12-man Queensland. Noted for his running game and his defence, he always looked the most dangerous player in the Blues’ attack and as the Maroons tired and the gaps began to open up he came into his own. Ethan Strange scored in a near-perfect debut for NSW. Getty Images Strange gained valuable experience on last year’s Kangaroos tour, where he mixed with NSW halfback Nathan Cleary, the man of the match on Wednesday night. Club coach Ricky Stuart had predicted Strange would be playing in the sky blue in the next year – but even the former Blues halfback would have been stunned by the maiden display.



He also had made some big hits in defence and will be tough to dislodge when Mitchell Moses recovers from a minor hamstring issue that forced him to withdraw on Tuesday. “That was pretty special, that one,” Strange said. “Playing with all these guys, they’re all legends of the game. I’m pinching myself.” Standing in the coaching box, Daley could only have been proud as one of the state’s best ever five-eighths. The NSW coach’s mood had been different for most of the game, as the Blues shot themselves in the foot with a catalogue of errors to open the way for Queensland to race to a 20-0 lead. But as Cleary stood up when it mattered, directing NSW to the stunning triumph, Daley was left celebrating.



He had been evasive about his future as Blues coach in the lead-up to this series, the second year of his second stint in charge of the state side. “I guarantee you, I know exactly what I want to do,” he said on his breakfast radio program. NSW coach Laurie Daley. Getty Images “There’s no surprise with what I’m doing. I know what my future looks like, but for me, I am headfirst into game one.” The strong suggestion has been that he would walk away from the job even if the Blues won.

World.title: Tourism operators brace for future after most weather-disrupted summer on record
World.content:
Photo: RNZ

Tourism operators are bracing for more frequent storms after some experienced their most weather-disrupted summer on record.

A storm hit Aotearoa every eight days on average between March last year and the end of February.

There is a common saying in the tourism industry - make hay while the sun shines.

The money operators make during a busy summer helps to see them through the quieter months.

But a flurry of destructive storms put a dampener on an otherwise strong summer.

EcoZip Adventures managing director Gavin Oliver said it was unfortunate timing.

"The weather's had a profound effect this year. In Kaikōura, we lost nine operating days in January to wet weather. So January is the strongest month of the year. So a third of January went west because of the weather," he said.

The weather also impacted his Waiheke Island zipline.

"We had two weeks of fairly consistent rain, which unfortunately depressed visitor numbers," he said.

"We're not thinking of weather so much as an operational challenge anymore. It's an economic impact. It's an economic challenge to be weathered."

He had already made changes to help make his businesses more resilient.

"At our Kaikōura location, generally we access our site through the Kahutara River. But when the river gets up, you don't want to put vehicles through it. So we've had to develop an off-road access, an alternative access road in.

"Now that's come at significant cost, but it's essential to the day-to-day operation of the business when you get those unexpected events."

Photo: Supplied / EcoZip Adventures

Kāpiti Island Nature Tours managing director John Barrett said it was the most weather disrupted summer in the 30 years he had been in business.

"We're like squirrels, I guess. We go through a good part of the year when there's no revenue being generated in our business because we're a predominantly summer business. We go like the clappers during the summer to provide as good a product as we possibly can and that generally results in a margin at the end of the season," he said.

"And if we're lucky, we're close to budget."

They were unlucky this summer and ended up slightly under-budget, he said.

"Traditionally, going back 20 or 30 years, if we lost three or four or five days in a season ... we'd accept that.

"This season, for example, we were losing four and five days at a stretch. I think we did that maybe three times."

It had a significant impact on his staff, business and reputation.

He wanted to see more action from the industry to ensure it was well prepared and could adapt to more frequent, severe weather.

Photo: Supplied: John Barrett

In Northland, Silver Wave Yacht Charters skipper and director Scott Farrand said even a few days of cancelling trips added up during summer.

They always needed to be vigilant and monitor forecasts throughout the day, moving boats to safer mooring waters when the conditions looked poor, he said.

Photo: Supplied / Silver Wave Yacht Charters

"There should be some more forward planning regarding how we are protecting the Bay of Islands, the tourism industry as a whole, and operators that aren't in the tourism industry for that matter, that do work in those low-lying areas that are affected by swells when they come in, washing out roads and accesses."

He was disappointed a controversial breakwater to protect Pihia foreshore and marina from storms fell through a few years ago.

Destination Hauraki Coromandel general manager Kylie Hawker-Green said summer was looking promising and then damaging rain hit during the Auckland Anniversary long weekend.

"Traditionally, one of our busiest weekends in the whole season, roads were closed and unfortunately visitors just couldn't get to us," she said.

"Since then we've had about half a dozen other weather events And unfortunately that's meant it's been quite a depressed summer season for our domestic visitors."

The January storm flooded some tourism businesses, cut power and forced some campsites to be evacuated, but she said most were covered by insurance.

They were also hit with a wave of cancellations.

"People were nervous about having a booking for a month or six weeks time because they weren't sure whether they could get there, if it was going to be open. And so many businesses have suffered loss of income or loss of forward income because of widespread cancellations as a result of those weather events," she said.

Photo: Supplied

The organisation had been working with businesses to create their own resilience plans, advocate for tax relief for those struggling and help others to understand what their insurance policies covered.

But she said it had been hard to shake the misconception that the peninsula was closed for business.

"I know that it's always a great headline to talk about a state of emergency and a road being closed. It doesn't ever get picked up that the road is now open and it's perfectly fine and safe to travel," she said.

"So we've had to do a lot of work in increasing our comms and our messaging out to wider audiences to remind people that we're here, we're open, we're trading and everything is good as gold."

Tourism Industry Aotearoa chief executive Rebecca Ingram said many of its businesses reported days when they could not operate during summer due to the weather.

The industry worked with Aotearoa Circle to create climate change scenarios and create an adaptation roadmap to help the sector be resilient and reduce the impact of climate change a few years ago, Ingram said.

More recently, she said it had been helping business to prepare with webinars, advice for crisis plans and communications, and longer weather forecasts for the summer.

"It affects resourcing, what you might think your investment strategy needs to be, the sort of things that you might need to adapt to in (the) future. How you have to build up your reserves in case you've got more days where you can't operate. It's cancellation policies, all of this is a factor and we're doing our best to help our members navigate it."

World.title: Disability advocates hope for transport, housing support in Budget
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Amy Williams

A vision impaired man who relies on taxis to get to work says a drop in the transport subsidy next month means he may have to move closer to his workplace in Auckland.

More than 120,000 elderly and disabled people rely on government transport subsidies through the Total Mobilty scheme, which are dropping from 75 percent to 65 percent from July.

Disability advocates hope Thursday's Budget will include transport and housing support for the community.

Milton Paul travels across Auckland in the early hours of each weekday in a taxi, to avoid congestion on his way to work.

He is blind in one eye and vision impaired in the other with no ability to see depth - public transport from Massey in the west to Homai in the south is not an option.

"It's super crucial, it's a service that I depend on to go to and from work. It's a service I've used since I was 18 years old."

It cost Paul $300 out of his own pocket for 10 taxi trips each week - the rest is funded through Total Mobility but that subsidy is about to drop by 10 percent.

"This has kind of caught me off guard a bit with this whole change, it's going to be a huge expense to me with the additional cost."

On Thursday, a taxi ride to the barber was on the cards but Paul said getting to work was his priority and he may have to move house to be closer to his workplace.

"For this to continue, there are things that I'm going to have to cut out or I may just have to move to a closer area but again that's a super struggle as it is."

He had not caught a bus or train for six years because he found it hard to board the correct service.

Official figures showed less than half of disabled people were in paid employment and for those who were working, the median income is $625 less than non-disabled.

Disability advocate Blake Forbes said reductions in the subsidy for taxi trips would force some to make tough decisions - to forgo trips to the doctor, supermarket or even work.

Photo: RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"I'm really concerned that people will be chosing between food and health," he said.

"I worry about disability employment that people won't be able to afford to get to work because it's so hard for disabled people to get employment, we've got one of the highest rates of unemployment in the country."

Forbes travels with Driving Miss Daisy which is applying a temporary surcharge to trips during the fuel crisis.

He said the Total Mobility subsidy helped to keep costs down but his own costs would rise when that reduced.

"I'm certainly going to have to pick and choose a bit more. I expect I'll be trying to stick around local things more or spacing my speaking engagements out a bit more so I can afford to take them."

Forbes and disability advocate Nick Ruane are working together to advocate for more support for people with disabilities - they are concerned an ongoing review of eligibility criteria for the Total Mobility scheme will lock some who need it out.

"The choice that disabled people are making is 'do I leave the house today, do I make that trip to the supermarket, do I make that trip to the doctor' and those are the choices that they are making already," Ruane said.

"This decision to limit who can go back into the scheme will make those choices even harder."

Ruane said it would come as a surprise to learn how much people who could not drive or take public transport spent on taxis - hundreds of dollars each week was common.

"The general public would be floored when they start hearing figures like that but that is not an unusual figure," he said.

"People are spending money in order to travel because public transport is not accessible to them and that's the only option available to them unfortunately."

For the blind and low vision community, 60 percent had annual incomes between $20,000 and $40,000.

Blind Low Vision chief executive Andrea Midgen said the cost of a taxi is already a big expense for many and the anticipated added cost when the subsidy reduces would force people to stay home more often.

Photo: Supplied / Blind Low Vision NZ

She wanted the government Budget to ensure the disabled community had the support they deserved to participate in society.

"It's super tough for our community. Often they can't get employment so they're on a benefit, they're struggling around $20,000 to $40,000 a year. Every single hit they get makes it even harder.

"We just want our community to have the supports that they deserve. Support to be able to be employed, support to be able to get to employment, support to have adequate housing that is accessible for our community."

Milton Paul would also like to see more support.

"It's almost at the point where you live pay cheque to pay cheque, it's almost like you have to have two incomes flowing in," he said.

"I'm just not sure why the disability sector is getting targeted this time around, in this Budget. I understand that maybe there's a lot of spending there but it is well needed especially in a space where we as low vision citizens are already at a huge disadvantage in life."

World.title: Raising a left-handed child in a right-handed world
World.content: Throughout history, left-handers have faced bias and been forced to convert to being right-handed for a range of reasons. These include cultural and religious ideas, with the left hand being associated with bad luck, and in some religions the use of the left hand considered a taboo.

World.title: Defence minister receives a single briefing regarding the Iran war
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The defence minister has received a single briefing regarding the Iran war - about shipping in the Persian Gulf - according to a new Official Information Act (OIA) response.

Chris Penk took over as minister from Judith Collins on 7 April, after serving as associate minister of defence.

RNZ asked for any briefings or similar to Penk as minister about the war - including anything related to the NZ Defence Force (NZDF) - or to its interactions with any partner or ally, including Australia and the US.

Penk's response was that one document was in scope for the OIA: a briefing in mid-April about an invite to the NZDF.

This invite was to a UK-led planning meeting about a multi-national approach to support freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

The briefing recommended Penk agree, because it would help the NZDF understand what might be done, and he could brief Cabinet and ministers on that.

It added that while it would be up to Cabinet whether to take part in any mission, if the public found out about NZDF going to the meeting that "could still give rise to the public perception that New Zealand has an intent to participate in military activity in the Strait of Hormuz".

If it did go along, officials would then "provide updated advice on public messaging that makes clear" it did not indicate a decision the country would take part in any multinational coalition "should one emerge".

A defensive multinational military mission has since been launched led by the UK and France. Britain is sending autonomous mine hunting equipment and counter-drone systems, it said.

World.title: Waitaki mayor Mel Tavendale concedes 22 percent rate hike will be a 'tough ask'
World.content:
Photo: Jackie Tav

The Waitaki mayor Mel Tavendale concedes it will be a "tough ask" for local residents to absorb a mammoth 22 percent rates hike.

Local councillors "reluctantly" agreed to the rates increase for the next financial year during an extraordinary Waitaki District Council meeting on Tuesday.

The council had been seeking feedback on three possible rates rises of 19 percent, 27 percent or a whopping 45 percent as it tried to plug a projected $14 million operating deficit.

A bleak financial forecast prompted calls from stunned ratepayers for a government probe of council's finances, due to fears people would lose their homes.

More than 500 submissions were received.

Speaking to RNZ, Tavendale said a 22 percent increase was not acceptable.

"We haven't been rating enough for a number of years to cover our actual operating costs. We've had deficits that we've accepted for the last nine out of 10 years as a council and essentially things are costing more than we have been bringing in rates."

An expensive water services programme had contributed to a huge increase in expenditure for local authorities.

Tavendale said it would be a struggle for residents.

"It's going to be a real tough ask. Essentially, our median income is 32,000 as a community, which is 10,000 less than the national average."

Photo: Supplied / Waitaki District Council

Concerns were raised during the meeting by councillor Mata'aga Hana Fanene-Taiti about the ability of residents absorbing costly rates bills.

"There are parts of the community that realistically won't be able to (pay). Have we considered what that gap could potentially be," she said.

In response, council support services director Paul Hope said the costs would ultimately be recouped because council "could sell properties".

Tavendale said although council could legally force the sale or lease of a property to recover unpaid rates, it was not standard practice.

"It's certainly not the direction we head down at all. We do whatever we can to not resort to anything like that," she said.

Council was exploring payment plan options for ratepayers, Tavendale said.

Photo: Supplied / Waitaki District Council

Councillor Jim Hopkins, who voted against the rates increase, said people were considering leaving the district altogether.

"Sorry, it's a monstrously huge amount," he said.

He said he had never seen more anger and concern over an issue than what he saw among the hundreds that attended a public meeting in Oamaru earlier this month.

Alongside the rates increase, other changes to the capital expenditure budget were also decided, including a $5.3m reduction in the water programme, a $1.2m increase in roading investment, and $383,000 in reductions across other budgets.

This would lower council's debt position, but not its operating deficit.

Further cuts to operating budgets for training, travel and catering totalling almost $100,000 were also agreed to.

World.title: Budget 26: Opposition, advocates have low expectations of support for those struggling most
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Liam Swiggs

The opposition is not expecting much in Thursday's Budget for those doing it toughest, but an economist says he would be surprised if there is not at least some nice surprises.

Finance Minister Nicola Willis is promising a careful balancing of the books and no big spendup, promising no lolly scramble.

"New Zealanders work hard for their money, and they expect the government to treat taxpayer dollars with care and discipline," she told Parliament in Wednesday's Question Time.

"Families across the country sit around their kitchen tables every week making difficult decisions about what they can afford and where they need to prioritise. Government should be held to the same standard."

But the Salvation Army warned those with the least were doing it toughest, its social policy director Bonnie Robinson warning the level of need at food banks was still 40 percent higher than before the Covid pandemic.

Photo: RNZ / Mark Papalii

She wanted to see more funding for them in the Budget, and did not accept tough economic conditions as an excuse.

"We've got the cost of living crisis and now we've got the fuel crisis - so if you're on a fixed income and a very tight budget now it's got tougher, so we really don't need anything that's going to make it more difficult for people.

"What we actually need to see is more assistance.

"Yes, it's tough economic times but a lot of our clients are making tough choices every single day about which bill to pay, can they feed themselves today, can the kids get what they need today, so we really need to make sure that those who have the least are not being asked to do it tougher."

She said the government's public service cuts were likely to add to the pressure, and the Reserve Bank's indication of higher inflation in future was a real worry for those on low incomes - who had no wriggle room left.

The Bank yesterday held the cash rate steady, but half the committee wanted to raise the rate in anticipation of higher inflation and ongoing uncertainty over fuel and the Iran war.

Economist Michael Reddell said the public service cuts - mostly set down for the years after the election - were what would be funding most of the new spending.

Photo: Supplied

"They were probably done at the last minute when they saw the first round of fiscals and saw with the weaker economy that surplus was probably receding even further into the future, so they sort of looked to have to pull together something pretty quickly to keep it in line.

"I suspect going into the election the government won't have wanted to allow that surplus target to drift any further.

"I think it really is political theater at the moment. I mean, this was announced last week with no substance, no specifics. Had it been worked up over months, almost certainly they would have had some specifics."

He said major changes to debt and surplus expectations were unlikely, but it would be surprising if there were no positive headlines from it.

"The way these things work is ministers get the numbers, look at what the implications are, and then from a political perspective there's the issue of what can you tolerate in terms of when you get back to surplus.

"That surplus state is blown out under both the previous government and this government almost a year every year - but I mean every Budget still has some rabbit in the hat that the minister has.

"Given the constraints on spending at the moment I imagine those will be pretty small but it is election year, so it'll be surprising if they didn't have something there to get a slightly positive headline."

The Budget was likely to be more inflationary than what the Reserve Bank had forecast, he said, but the Monetary Policy Committee would have seen Willis' announcement of lower operational spending and higher capital spending, and those comments would have been taken into account.

He welcomed the Bank's increased transparency with the voting record of members of the Monetary Policy Committee publicly shared.

That happened for the first time on Wednesday - with the external members all voting to increase the cash rate - and Reddell said that was a trend that was undesirable, but at least it could now be judged.

"One of the suspicions has always been that having internal members, some of them could be swayed by the Governor - ultimately they work for the Governor - and you'd like to see sort of diversity of view within both the externals and the internals.

"Now we can sort of hold them to account for their judgments as things go forward, recognising that there's always a huge amount of uncertainty, and that no member of the Monetary Policy Committee will ever always get it right."

World.title: Scientists not holding out hope for big Budget boost after year of cuts and sector overhaul
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Mark Papalii

Scientists are adamant investing in the sector now will pay dividends later - but are not holding out much hope for a big Budget funding boost after a year of redundancies and funding cuts amid a major overhaul of the sector.

Last year saw the biggest shake-up to the science system in 30 years.

It saw Crown Research Institutes merge into Public Research Organisations, the scrapping of Callaghan Innovation, and a raft of new intiatives including: the establishment of the Gene Technology Regulator, an office to attract foreign investment, and an advisory council to the prime minister.

Budget 2025 cannibalised research and innovation funds to help fund the changes.

Minister of Science, Innovation and Technology Penny Simmonds would not comment on Thursday's Budget, but said researchers make an "extraordinary contribution" and the sector's significant reforms would create a more stable, strategic, and sustainable system.

Innovate or 'death spiral' - researcher

Lincoln Agritech chief executive Travis Glare said the sector's recent upheaval needed to be followed by stability and long-term vision.

"There's been real cuts to the science system over the last few years, which means the system struggles as you're basically losing people. You've got amalgamated science organisations - that takes a lot of money to merge organisations - and that's all money that's not going into actually doing the science."

Photo: Supplied / Lincoln Agritech

He hoped Budget 2026 would redirect money into research and development [R&D] - his company's core purpose - and 'blue-skies' or curiosity-driven research to enable a "discovery pipeline".

Glare said investing in science over more tangible public services could be a difficult argument for taxpayers, but he said long-term economic success hinged on innovation - and that required years of work.

"We're not actually building an economy that will pay for better healthcare and better education. The government is having to divide a much smaller pie every year and innovation is the only way we're getting out of this death spiral."

Glare said after years of what felt like "ad hoc" funding - a strategy for the sector was a brightspot.

"Not everyone is going to agree with it, but at least reseachers understand what the government is looking for."

In its report to the prime minister earlier this year, the Science and Technology Advisory Council outlined a framework for the government to signal investment priorities. It was based on four 'pillars' covering primary industries, environmental sustainability, technology, and health.

It said the country's poor economic performance reflected "deep-seated structural and external challenges" and targeted public investment in science, innovation, and technology [SI&T] offered "one of the most direct and high-impact pathways to restore momentum".

"This is reinforced by overwhelming international evidence that SI&T are core to lifting productivity, export competitiveness and economic growth.

"The country's scientists, researchers and entrepreneurs deliver strong results within the system's constraints, but barriers continue to limit their impact."

It urged the government to scale up investment once the framework proved its capability.

Photo: Waikato University

Co-president of the New Zealand Association of Scientists Troy Baisden said business R&D had flatlined recently, indicating the public system was not adequately supporting private investment and believed New Zealand did not appreciate the link between science R&D and productivity.

"There's a lack of a sense that much of our agricultural productivity came from investments 20-30 years ago in science."

He said small gains in the sector over the past year had been overshadowed by bigger losses and hoped the overhaul in the sector created a system that politicians could confidently invest in.

But optimism for this Budget was tempered.

"What we're really looking for at this point are no more cuts."

'Everything you touch came through ... research'

McDiarmid Institute director Nicola Gaston said she was not expecting much in the Budget, but after a year characterised by disruption a commitment to boost funding - down the line - would be welcome.

Photo: Victoria University

"In the absense of new money this year, a plan to grow investment over time and ... more information about the process of funding so that it has a level of visibility to researchers [would be good].

"That level of uncertainty I think has created some level of distrust of the process, so I'd like to see more detail and something that looks like an actual plan."

Gaston said research funding, or "baseline funding for universities" was essential if the country wanted a workforce capable of navigating a "rapidly changing world".

"You need to have a functional research-informed education system, that means you need to fund research."

Auckland University associate professor of sociology Sereana Naepi agreed, maintaining there would be no Rocket Lab without a healthy education and undergraduate research pipeline.

Photo: Supplied

But she acknowledged investing in such a system could be a hard sell for the public given a lot of the work was unseen.

"But everything you touch came through the research space at some point and so while we're not an immediate day-to-day thing in a lot of people's minds, if you like your phone, if you like your computer, if you like immunisations or if you like that ability to put a stent in your heart - it usually came out of the research sector before it got privatised."

Long-term direction promised

Science Minister Penny Simmonds - the third to hold the portfolio this government term - said the science reforms were focussed on getting the settings right so public investment "delivers stronger impact, with clearer priorities and better connections to industry".

She said R&D continued to be supported through public investment and tools like the R&D Tax Incentive.

"Which is helping lift business investment in innovation, which is extremely important as two-thirds of the R&D that happens in New Zealand takes place in private businesses.

"The upcoming Science Investment Plan will set out the Government's long-term direction for science, innovation and technology and will provide greater certainty for the sector."

She said she was unable to comment on what may or may not be included in the Budget ahead of Budget Day.

"However, what I can say is, New Zealand's researchers make an extraordinary contribution and deserve a system that supports excellence and stability."

World.title: Wellington councillor still at loggerheads with mayor over search and rescue
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Mark Papalii

A Wellington councillor who quit a sub-committee a week ago is still at loggerheads with the city mayor over his involvement at a search and rescue operation during Wellington's floods.

Wharangi/Onslow-Western Ward councillor Ray Chung resigned as chair of the Council Controlled Organisations subcommittee earlier this month.

Chung was at the search area for missing Karori man Philip Sutton on 21 April, who was swept away in floodwaters, after friends of Sutton's family issued a call for volunteers on a day police had suspended their search. Police later urged the public not to take the search into their own hands.

Mayor Andrew Little said Chung was told before he attended the scene that the search was a police matter. Ultimately, he should not have got involved in a search operation, Little said.

"Cr Chung told me he was being contacted by people who had concerns about the missing person search. I told him the search was a police matter. I told the councillor to contact the Police Area Commander."

A week on from his resignation, Chung maintains he was not getting involved in the search, and he stood by his actions.

He said he was only heading to the scene to try and prevent volunteers from getting in harm's way, after finding out members of the public were getting involved in the search.

He would not speak to why he resigned from the subcomittee.

"I absolutely wasn't getting involved in the search, the mayor knows it, the police know it.

"All I did, was I was doing what I think councillors should be doing, is looking after their constituents, when their constituents need help, you go and see what you can do to help them."

Chung sent an email, which RNZ has seen, in which he told council officers and the mayor he was going to the scene to try to stop people going into the water there.

Chung said he did not have the area commander's phone number, so he contacted a police officer from the search and rescue unit, who told him he did not want volunteers doing their own search, and asked Chung to tell them not to get involved.

Police have not confirmed that version of events.

Little said a senior member of police, Wellington Area Comander Dean Silvester, contacted him about Chung's involvement in the search - including "inappropriate contact" the councillor had made by speaking with the head of the search and rescue unit, Little said.

"He contacted me through text to say he was concerned about it, we had a conversation, I took those issues up with Ray, we had ongoing discussions. I have to say my priority at the time was getting council's response, sorting people out and getting rubbish collections and all that sort of stuff - and I did say it wouldn't be my top priority at the time."

Little said he later spoke with Chung, and "expressed a lack of confidence in him", and Chung subsequently chose to resign.

When asked why Chung's behaviour was concerning, Little said: "We were in a state of emergency, there was a search that the police had commenced but had suspended for safety reasons, and he along with others, had chosen to get involved and resume the search when it was contrary to the police's guidance and direction."

Little said the issue was over as far as he was concerned.

"That's it, from my point of view, to the extent I had concerns, the issue's now been disposed of, because he's no longer in a responsible role.

Wellington Area Commander Inspector Dean Silvester said he spoke with the mayor during the week of Wellington's severe weather, which is "normal in such an event".

"No complaint was made."

World.title: Maroons let 20-0 lead slip in Origin I after Kalyn Ponga sent off late
World.content:
James Tedesco has scored a spectacular try with 90 seconds left in State of Origin I to cap off a stunning comeback to win State of Origin I 22-20 at a sodden Stadium Australia.

An electric Queensland outfit shot out to a 20-0 lead after 20 minutes of the series opener in Sydney, before spending an hour desperately trying to cling on.

That task was made harder when superstar fullback Kalyn Ponga was sent off for a shoulder charge on a flying Tolu Koula after 57 minutes.

Loading Instagram content

Cameron Munster and Ponga insisted that it was the fullback's head, not his shoulder, that hit Koula high.

But Ashley Klein would not be moved, noting Ponga's shoulder-charge action before making the Newcastle fullback the seventh man to be sent off in an Origin match, although not everyone agreed.

"I'm still in shock about the Kalyn Ponga decision," Queensland legend Darren Lockyer said on Channel Nine after the game.

Kalyn Ponga had played a sensational game until his blunder. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"Credit to New South Wales, but there will be plenty of people north of the border who will struggle to accept that decision."

The score at that stage was 20-6 for Queensland but the send off completely changed the complexion of the contest.

Debutant Ethan Strange and halfback Nathan Cleary scored on 62 and 71 minutes, as the Maroons' defence scrambled in the wet.

They repelled the Blues until the final moments, when Cleary's bomb landed a metre in front of the tryline and Tedesco outleapt Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, pinched the ball, juggled and regathered on the way to grounding.

James Tedesco scored a miracle try in the final 90 seconds to win the game for the Blues. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"That was unreal, a bit surreal to be honest," Tedesco, the reigning Dally M medallist who was playing his first Origin match since Game I of 2024.

"We dug deep, we knew we'd get some opportunities.

"We made too many errors [in the first half] … we made it hard for ourselves.

"We had plenty of opportunities and I'm just glad I came up with something."

Cleary potted the extras from just next to the posts and NSW took a 1-0 series lead before the series heads to Melbourne for Game II in three weeks' time.

The Blues will celebrate tonight, but will be left wondering how Queensland got such a jump on them in the opening exchanges.

Uncharacteristic errors from Brian To'o and Stephen Crichton didn't help the Blues, but the Maroons were utterly irresistible for the first half hour of the game.

Tom Flegler was swarmed by his teammates after scoring a try in his return to the Origin arena. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Robert Toia, Thomas Flegler and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow all scored in the opening 16 minutes of the match, with Sam Walker playing brilliantly on debut, kicking four goals from four.

But the Blues scored off their very first foray into the Maroons end, Hudson Young scoring off a magical kick by Nathan Cleary, who was later awarded player of the match honours.

They Blues could have had a second before the break only for Cameron Murray to be penalised for a foul before grounding in the in-goal.

The game evolved into an arm wrestle early in the second half, before Ponga's crucial collision, which resulted in Koula being subbed out of the game with a concussion and Ponga fined 23 per cent of his match fee.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

Live updates State of Origin Game I S By Simon Smale Collapse all posts off Sort Sort posts Latest Select an option New: Filters Choose what information you see below by using filters Filter Posts All 124 Key Events 19 Tries 7 Goals 1 Comments 12 All filters Time to say goodbye S By Simon Smale (Getty Images) Well, a stunning victory for the Blues, as dramatic as it could possibly be, with the people's champion James Tedesco scoring the winner on his return to the Origin stage. Genuinely couldn't happen to a nicer guy. As far as Queensland will be concerned, that was one that got away. To be 20-0 up and still lose the game, no matter the circumstances, is a failure and puts the defending champions on the back foot heading to the MCG next month. Was the Ponga send off correct? I think it depends on who you are talking to. The fact is that Tolu Koula was unable to resume the match after the incident due to the contact. There is also, from the alternative side, that Ashley Klein overruled the Bunker official who told him the incident did not meet the threshold for a send off. That conversation will rumble on and on. But, for now, our conversation is over. Thanks so much for being with us on a soggy night in capitals either side of the border. Until we meet again, at the MCG on June 17. 'The Blues don't win that game unless Ponga gets sent off': Paul Gallen S By Simon Smale Paul Gallen is speaking on Channel Nine at the moment. He is pretty adamant that the Blues were the second best team on the ground throughout the opening exchanges. He says that the Blues may even need to make a couple of changes ahead of the second game. "The Blues don't win that game unless Ponga gets sent off," Ponga says. "I think they need to keep a lid on it and pick a team that can win Game II because you do not want to go up to Queensland for a decider." Murray credits Blues pressure S By Simon Smale Cameron Murray is speaking now to Channel Nine. He still looks to be in a bit of shock about how the game was turned around so late. He is asked about what the Blues did well when the Maroons were down to 12 men, and he says that it was basically just their pressure. "We probably just did a great job with building pressure," Murray says. "We just put a bit more fatigue in their defensive line." They sure did - the Blues dominated late on, at one stage earning seven sets in a row against the Maroons increasingly desperate defence. Daley won't be drawn on the Ponga decision J By Jon Healy The NSW coach is asked about Kalyn Ponga being sent off the field. "I'd rather not say," he says. I'll leave it to you to decipher that. Does he want to avoid being panned for kicking a bloke when he's down or did he disagree with the call? I think more likely the former, but he's not given us much to go off. Captain Isaah Yeo says he thinks it was a send-off, but admits he's hardly an impartial observer. "Bias says I think it's a send off. We've been on that side of it as well. I don't know." Daley says this is nothing new. "If you look through Origin history there's always been moment and there's always been wins like that; you take 'em." Slater's pride J By Jon Healy Slater pretty much always talks about being proud of his team, but you can tell there's a little more feeling behind it tonight. "We've gotta take some positives out of what we did tonight, and there were a lot. "It's natural to feel heartbroken and disappointed but we won't be throwing the baby out with the bath water." The coach is asked what he's most proud of. "The heart and spirit they fought with. "Twenty-three minutes in a State of Origin game with 12 men, they fought hard. You could see they were just holding on in stages. "One moment at the end of the game it could be a different story, but it's not. "I'm sure all Queenslanders are proud of their footy team right now." 'I suggest you ask someone else': Gould refuses to talk about send off S By Simon Smale The Channel Nine team are talking about the send off. There are mixed feelings. "We could hear the thump [sideline]," Darren Lockyer says. "I looks sickening from a distance. "And I think Ashley Klein always had this [the send off] in his mind. "The Bunker said it should be 10 minutes ... but Ashley Klein didn't have a bar of it." Brad Fittler is more accepting of the call. "As the defender, you have responsibility ... you have to be on the down side," Fittler says. "That's why he was sent off." As for what Gus Gould thinks? He pleads the fifth. "I suggest you ask someone else, not me," Gus Gould says. Interesting. "He's probably thinking he's cost the team the game," Lockyer says. "There will be a lot of people in the changing room at the moment, who will be perplexed at how that happened." Billy Slater has no problems with Kalyn Ponga send-off J By Jon Healy Queensland coach Billy Slater says the decision to send Kalyn Ponga off "is what it is". "I haven't got any problems with it. "I'm not gonna make any noise about it. They're the breaks." He says Ponga "obviously feels like he let his team down". Captain Cameron Munster says he felt like the speed of the incident and the fact Ponga tried to get low with Tolu Koula, plus the head-to-head contact, might have meant it was only a sin-bin. "I thought it might have been head on head but the ref and the bunker saw it differently. Those are the rules. Ref's gotta make a split decision." Strange 'sparked' the Blues: Johns S By Simon Smale Andrew Johns says Ethan Strange "sparked" the Blues. "You're looking at a guy who may play 30 Origins," he says. "After KP got sent off and the field opened up, he was "devastating Cameron Smith agrees. "I agree," he says.

"It was a wonderful debut." Darren Lockyer 'in shock' over Ponga send off S By Simon Smale Here is Queensland legend Darren Lockyer. He is very, very unhappy. "I'm still in shock about the Kalyn Ponga decision," he says. "Credit to New South Wales, but there will be plenty of people north of the border who will struggle to accept that decision." Young 'proud' of Strange S By Simon Smale Hudson Young is being interviewed now on Nine. "I am so proud of Ethan," he says. :First time he stepped on the field you knew he would be an Origin player, and he stepped up tonight." Gould: 'The first 25 minutes was everything I feared' S By Simon Smale "The first 25 minutes was everything I feared," says Gus Gould on Nine. "They started the second half pretty positively. "There was some really magical individual moments. I don't want playing against 12 men to take away from what he [Nathan Cleary] did under very difficult conditions. 'Greatest' Origin comeback ever? S By Simon Smale How can the NSW origin win be called the greatest come back win, when NSW played against 10 men for the greater part of the 2nd half? Poor decision by the referee against the spirit of state of origin rugby, that may set a precedent for future origin games. Ridiculous call! - Victorian Dale Not sure you can call it the “greatest origin comeback” when it’s a home game and 13 vs 12…. - Lj The blues played terribly for a team that was a man up for a quarter of the game. When Ponga went off I was expecting a blow out - Josh So NSW can win an Origin! (Against 12) - Muzz 'A different level': Haumole Olakau'atu S By Simon Smale Haumole Olakau'atu is speaking to ABC Sport too. He could have won the game much earlier for the Blues only to drop the ball with a three-man overlap. "I should've caught that but as I bent over to catch the ball everything just locked up and that was my night," he says. "Bad pass or not you still gotta execute and it wasn't good enough from my end. "I'm just glad Tedesco did that. If it was anyone else I don't know whether they would've pulled it off. "All these talks about the speed of the game is next level and it was no joke. This … is a different level." 'They're a hard enough team to defend when you've got a full team': Capewell S By Simon Smale (@ABCSport) Kurt Capewell has been speaking to ABC Sport too. "Definitely disappointing. We set the game up well and to lose like that hurts, but that's footy," he says. "They're a hard enough team to defend when you've got a full team out there, let alone 12 men. "We'll learn from it." To quote Nathan Cleary, 'Origin, hey?' S By Simon Smale One of the great Origins. Not a perfect performance - probably one of the worst from a winning side in Origin - but holy hell what a ride. - Tom Tedesco: 'Nath ... was instrumental' S By Simon Smale (@ABCSport) Here's some more from James Tedesco, speaking to ABC Sport. "That was unreal, a bit surreal to be honest," he says. "We dug deep, we knew we'd get some opportunities. I bombed one earlier so I knew I had to make up for it. "We made too many errors [in the first half], it was very slippery, we made it hard for ourselves in the first half. "We had plenty of opportunities and I'm just glad I came up with something. "Nath put it on the spot. He was instrumental. Strangey was unreal." Sam Walker doesn't want to talk S By Simon Smale Sam Walker is speaking now. He doesn't want to but is being told he has to as the Channel Nine cameras pursue him across the Sydney turf. "It's a hard one to reflect on right now," he says. "Just disappointed I guess. "It's really special to be able to put the jersey on," he adds, looking anything but happy. 'It's just Origin, hey?' Nathan Cleary is man of the match S By Simon Smale Nathan Cleary sums up most of our thoughts about that game. "It's just Origin, hey?" he says. "Queensland got the jump on us, but a lot of the talk behind the line was really positive. "Obviously pretty disappointed with that first half, not much defensive resilience." Ethan Strange 'that was pretty special' S By Simon Smale Ethan Strange is speaking now. "That was pretty special that one," he says. "Playing with all these guys, they're legends of the game. "How about Nathan Cleary? "The way he manages the game is incredible." He says it was a blur of a match. He genuinely looks stunned to be out there still, living his dream. Show more posts
